independent_execution.note: Byte-equal to the committed test_output.txt. Four tests, all real, all passing.

hidden_cases.rationale: The most direct way to orphan lineage in a five-decision vocabulary that includes DELETE: delete the predecessor while a successor still names it. The frozen deliverable requires the compiler to enforce lineage continuity, so this is not an exotic input - it is the first thing the vocabulary makes possible.
hidden_cases.construction: Two routes: {route_id: old, decision: DELETE} and {route_id: new, decision: SUPERSEDE, predecessor_route_id: old}.
hidden_cases.interpretation: Accepted with no complaint. The compiler's only lineage test is whether the predecessor id appears as a key in the input set - it never consults that predecessor's own disposition. So a compiled plan can simultaneously delete a route and record another route as superseding it, which is exactly the lineage break the deliverable says must be refused. The negative control HC-A2, identical but with the predecessor RETAINed, is also ACCEPTED, so the compiler cannot distinguish the safe case from the unsafe one at all.

hidden_cases.rationale: Lineage continuity implies an origin. The producer explicitly blocks self-precedence, which shows awareness of the cycle class, so the question is whether the check has any depth.
hidden_cases.construction: Two routes forming a cycle: a SUPERSEDEs b, b SUPERSEDEs a. Then a three-route cycle a<-c, b<-a, c<-b.
hidden_cases.observed_output_verbatim:
HC-B  two-route lineage CYCLE (a<-b, b<-a)
HC-B: ACCEPTED
   accepted lineage: [('a', 'b'), ('b', 'a')]
HC-B2 three-route lineage CYCLE (a<-b<-c<-a)
HC-B2: ACCEPTED
hidden_cases.interpretation: Both cycles compile clean. The 'route cannot precede itself' guard is a cycle check of depth exactly one; there is no reachability or topological pass behind it. A compiled cycle has no origin record, which means the output can assert a lineage that cannot be walked - the precise failure mode 'enforces lineage continuity' names. The producer got close enough to this to write the depth-1 case and then stopped.

hidden_cases.rationale: Coverage. The hypothesis enumerates five decisions; the producer's tests exercise two valid ones plus one invalid one. RETEST, REJECT and DELETE appear in the frozen hypothesis and in the DECISIONS set but in no test.
hidden_cases.construction: Three routes carrying RETEST, REJECT and DELETE respectively.
hidden_cases.interpretation: All three work. The gap is only in test coverage, and since the check is a single frozenset membership test the untested decisions cannot behave differently. Low severity, recorded for completeness: the test named test_compiles_all_decisions_and_preserves_lineage in fact compiles two of the five.

hidden_cases.rationale: The word 'exactly' in the hypothesis. Two ways to carry more than one decision: declare the route twice, or put a list in the decision field.
hidden_cases.construction: (1) route_id 'dup' declared twice with RETAIN and DELETE. (2) a single route whose decision is the list ['RETAIN', 'DELETE'].
hidden_cases.observed_output_verbatim:
HC-D: REFUSED(DispositionError) | duplicate route_id: dup
HC-D2: CRASH(TypeError) | unhashable type: 'list'
hidden_cases.interpretation: Exactly-one is genuinely enforced against the realistic attack. The duplicate route_id refusal is clean and its message names the offending id. The list-valued decision raises TypeError from the frozenset membership test rather than DispositionError, so it fails closed but ungracefully - a hardening note, not a hole, since TypeError still aborts the compile.

hidden_cases.rationale: Malformed input sweep, to see whether refusals are typed and deliberate or incidental.
hidden_cases.construction: Route entries as plain strings; decision None; route_id an int; predecessor an int; empty route set.
hidden_cases.observed_output_verbatim:
route entries are plain strings      -> CRASH(ValueError)
   decision is None                     -> REFUSED(DispositionError)
   route_id is an int                   -> REFUSED(DispositionError)
   predecessor is an int                -> REFUSED(DispositionError)
   empty route set                      -> ACCEPTED
hidden_cases.interpretation: Type validation is real and typed for the field-level cases - the compiler checks isinstance on route_id and on predecessor rather than only truthiness. The string-entry case raises bare ValueError from dict(), but DispositionError subclasses ValueError so a caller catching ValueError is unaffected. The empty route set compiles to an empty plan, which is defensible for a validator.

hidden_cases.rationale: The producer's tests import compile_dispositions directly and never invoke the command-line entry point, so main(), the output-file path and the process-level exit codes are entirely untested. Reproducibility across fresh processes also has to be shown rather than assumed.
hidden_cases.construction: Ran disposition_compiler.py as a subprocess with a routes file and -o, twice into different output files, then once against a file containing an invalid decision.
hidden_cases.observed_output_verbatim:
exit=0 output_written=True
   deterministic ordering: ['a-first', 'z-last']
   second fresh-process run byte-identical: True
   CLI refusal path exit code on bad input:
   exit=1 traceback=True
hidden_cases.interpretation: The CLI works, sorts deterministically by route_id irrespective of input order, and two independent fresh-process runs produced byte-identical files. Refusal exits 1. The refusal surfaces as an uncaught traceback rather than a clean diagnostic, which is cosmetic for a validator but means an operator sees a stack trace instead of the lineage problem.

hidden_cases.rationale: The commission's stub-substitution test, run in both directions because a validator can be faked either by always refusing or by never checking.
hidden_cases.construction: Two stubs, each dropped in place of disposition_compiler.py with the producer's test file unchanged: (1) compile_dispositions always raises DispositionError with a message containing all three regex fragments the tests match on; (2) compile_dispositions performs no validation at all and just returns the routes sorted.
hidden_cases.observed_output_verbatim:
always-raise stub: exit=1 (rejects stub)
   always-accept stub: exit=1 (rejects stub)
hidden_cases.interpretation: NOT VACUOUS, and this is the unit's real strength. The test suite pins both directions - one test requires successful compilation and three require typed refusals - so neither a constant-refuse nor a constant-accept implementation survives it. This is the discipline unit 024 lacked, achieved with four short tests.

hidden_cases.interpretation: Mixed and worth reading carefully. The exactly-one-decision half of the hypothesis is TRUE at real scale and I verified it - 316 genuine changed routes, one decision each, no collisions, deterministic ordering. That evidence did not exist before this review. The preserved-lineage half fails on real data for the same reason it failed on synthetic data in HC-A: a real path DELETEd while another real path still names it as predecessor compiles without complaint.

hidden_cases.interpretation: Two findings, one about this unit and one about the wave. First: artifact-001 is CPython-3.12-specific bytecode that embeds the producer's absolute worktree path /home/ubuntu/po03-worktrees/c5/... - a machine-bound, interpreter-version-locked binary declared as a first-class deliverable inside a commission about portable runtime. Second, and more useful: the tree at that commit holds 290 blobs under workstreams/po03, of which unit 003's detector scanned 289 as text and skipped exactly 1 as binary. That one skipped blob is the only pyc in the tree, and it is the only artifact in the entire commit that actually contains an absolute producer path. So the wave's own non-portable-path detector reported 281 findings while stepping over the single true positive. This is real-repository confirmation of the coverage gap I recorded against unit 003 on synthetic grounds.

producer_declared_limitations: The compiler validates supplied route records; it does not infer dispositions for routes absent from the input.
scope_honesty_assessment.assessment: The one declared limitation is true and non-trivial - it concedes that 'assigns' in the deliverable is really 'validates', which is honest. But it is the only limitation declared, and the three things a reviewer most needs to know are absent from it: that lineage continuity is enforced only against dangling references and not against cycles or deleted predecessors, that three of the five decisions in the hypothesis are never exercised by a test, and that no fixture anywhere in the unit is a real PO-03 route. The manifest evidence line is accurate about what the tests covered - 'valid compilation, orphaned and missing predecessors, and unknown decisions' - which is a fair description of four tests but a thin basis for a hypothesis quantified over every changed route.

nonportable_artifacts_in_subtree: __pycache__/disposition_compiler.cpython-312.pyc - 3839 bytes, committed at 402c277618bcf4ba659588381f11b8fadf4e7424 and declared as manifest artifact-001. Interpreter-version-locked and embeds the absolute producer path /home/ubuntu/po03-worktrees/c5/workstreams/po03/attempts/po03-wa-b2e7-033-disposition-compiler/disposition_compiler.py. Mitigating: the producer removed it in a later commit on the same branch and added a .gitignore covering __pycache__/ and *.py[cod], so the cohort head tree is clean and the head .gitignore is itself an undeclared file in the subtree.
reproducibility_check: Reproducible and deterministic. Two independent fresh-process CLI runs on the same input produced byte-identical output, and output ordering is sorted by route_id rather than input order.
divergence_reason: The frozen deliverable names three obligations and one of them is not met. 'Enforces lineage continuity' fails against two inputs I built in a few lines each: a two-route cycle and a three-route cycle both compile clean (HC-B), and a route may be DELETEd while another route still names it as predecessor (HC-A), which I reproduced on real repository paths as well as synthetic ones (HC-H). The compiler's entire lineage check is whether the predecessor id is a key in the input map; it never asks what disposition that predecessor itself carries, and its cycle guard has depth exactly one. The hypothesis' 'with preserved lineage' clause therefore does not hold as implemented. I record NOT_YET rather than FAIL because everything else here is sound and the gap is additive rather than structural - the exactly-one-decision half of the hypothesis is true and I confirmed it at real scale on 316 genuine changed routes, which is evidence the unit itself never produced. A reachability pass over the predecessor graph plus a check that a referenced predecessor is not DELETEd would close the gap without redesign.
disposition_reason: Rejected for one specific unmet clause of the frozen deliverable, not for quality. This is competent work: the validation is typed rather than truthy, checking isinstance on both route_id and predecessor; the duplicate-route_id refusal genuinely enforces the 'exactly one' in the hypothesis; the empty-input and self-precedence edge cases are handled; output is deterministically sorted and byte-identical across fresh processes; and unusually for this wave the four-test suite is non-vacuous in both directions - I substituted a constant-refuse stub and a no-validation stub and the suite rejected both. Set against that, 'enforces lineage continuity' is a named requirement in the frozen deliverable and it is not enforced: cycles pass and deleted predecessors pass, both demonstrated on real repository paths, and neither is disclosed in the unit's limitations. Two secondary items weigh in. The unit declares a CPython-3.12 bytecode blob as artifact-001 which embeds the producer's absolute worktree path, inside a commission whose subject is portable runtime; the producer did clean it up in a later commit and add a .gitignore, so I treat it as a lapse corrected rather than a live defect. And no fixture in the unit is a real PO-03 route, so a hypothesis quantified over every changed route rests on two-element toys - I supplied the real 316-route run myself and it succeeded, which is why the re-run should be short. Add a predecessor-graph reachability check, refuse a SUPERSEDE whose predecessor is DELETEd, exercise RETEST and REJECT, and run the compiler once over the real changed-route list, and this earns a clean PASS.
followups_for_coordinator: BLOCKING for re-run: refuse a plan in which a route named as predecessor_route_id carries the DELETE decision. Reviewer-observed: [{old, DELETE}, {new, SUPERSEDE, predecessor old}] compiles clean, and so does the same shape with real repository paths.

BLOCKING for re-run: add a reachability or topological pass over predecessor_route_id. Reviewer-observed: a<-b, b<-a and a three-route cycle all compile clean. The existing 'route cannot precede itself' guard is a depth-1 special case of exactly this check.

Run the compiler once over the real changed-route list rather than only two-element fixtures. I did this and it worked - 316 real changed paths between controller head 5cfebfdb and the c5 branch, one decision each, ACCEPTED - so this is cheap to satisfy and converts the hypothesis from asserted to demonstrated.

WAVE-LEVEL, cross-referenced with my unit 003 review: unit 003's non-portable-path detector scanned 289 of the 290 blobs under workstreams/po03 at commit 402c2776, skipped 1 as binary, and reported 281 findings - and the single skipped blob is the only artifact in that commit containing an absolute producer path. The detector stepped over the one true positive in the tree. This is real-repository confirmation of the coverage gap I recorded against unit 003 and it strengthens the case for re-running that unit with binary blobs in scope.
